Photograph: Anjum Naveed/AP Imran Khan Jailed ex-Pakistani PM Imran Khan in hospital after uproar over health Supreme court ordered transfer of ex-leader whose health is reportedly deteriorating and following public protests Shah Meer Baloch in Islamabad Thu 20 Aug 2026 19.07 EDT First published on Thu 20 Aug 2026 17.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Pakistan’s jailed former prime minister Imran Khan has been taken to a hospital in the country’s capital on supreme court orders after weeks of uproar about his deteriorating health. A spokesperson for Khan’s party, Zulfikar Bukhari, said: “Imran Khan has been shifted from Adiala jail to International Shifa hospital in Islamabad following the supreme court’s order.” Bukhari said that as per the court order, family should be allowed to meet Khan. “The next phase must therefore go beyond Imran Khan’s immediate medical treatment. It must ensure independent medical oversight, access to qualified specialists, respect for family and legal rights, and complete transparency regarding his health,” Bukhari said. Security was beefed up in Islamabad, and hundreds of security personnel were posted around the hospital before Khan was taken there. Prisoner number 804: the plot to erase Imran Khan – podcast Read more The government had to comply with the order by a three-judge panel of the supreme court that ordered the government to take Khan to the private hospital within 48 hours to be examined by physicians. Initially, the government seemed divided on whether to do so or not. Khan has been suffering from health issues including poor eyesight, and his family and party have been demanding he has access to specialist medical care for months. The family eventually took the case to the supreme court. In February, officials at Khan’s party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf, said he was facing severe eye damage and had only 15% eyesight, and was being kept in solitary confinement. He was also being denied basic medical care and meetings with family and lawyers. For months, Adiala jail has been a protest site, where Khan’s family and dozens of protesters would gather to demand medical care for him and for him to be allowed to meet his sisters. On Tuesday the judges said that they would involve an eye specialist for Khan’s treatment. The order read: “We are mindful of the constitutional and legal obligation … to safeguard the life, health, dignity and security of the prisoner.” Khan’s party assured the judges that his supporters would not gather in front of the hospital and would allow treatment to go smoothly. In the early hours of Friday, Asad Qaiser, the former speaker of the national assembly and a close aide of Khan, wrote on X that it had been decided by the party that no worker would gather in front of the hospital after Khan is taken to Shifa. He wrote “if anyone attempts to gather in front of the hospital and violating the party’s decision, he would have no affiliation with the party.” Khan was arrested in 2023 and sentenced to three years in jail on corruption charges and disqualified from politics for five years. Khan, who is facing more than 100 cases, was sentenced to 14 years in 2025 on corruption charges and accused of obtaining lucrative plots of land worth billions of rupees through a corrupt deal with a Pakistani property tycoon when he was the prime minister. Khan and his party denied the charges and said cases were politically motivated. He was Pakistan’s cricket captain before becoming a politician, and served as the prime minister of Pakistan from 2018 to 2022. He was ousted in a vote of no confidence. Khan had enjoyed good relations with Pakistan’s powerful military before he came to power. Once he was removed from office in 2022, he blamed the US for his removal initially and then Pakistan’s then army chief Gen Bajwa. Both have denied his accusations. After his brief arrest and release in May 2023, Khan in an interview with the Guardian accused Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir of harbouring a “personal grudge” against him and ordering his arrest and a crackdown on his party. Photograph: Mark Thomas/Alamy Metropolitan police Thirteenth Met police officer sacked after undercover BBC investigation PC Mason O’Connor dismissed following Panorama film showing misogyny and racism at London police station Yassin El-Moudden Tue 15 Sep 2026 18.59 EDT Last modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 19.25 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A 13th serving Metropolitan police officer has been dismissed in relation to an undercover BBC investigation into misogyny and racism at Charing Cross police station. PC Mason O’Connor was found to have committed discreditable conduct and breached professional behaviour standards, linked to a comment he made towards a female colleague, according to the Met. The Panorama investigation aired in October 2025 and followed seven months of undercover filming. It included footage of officers calling for immigrants to be shot and boasting about using violence against suspects. On Tuesday, a disciplinary panel heard that O’Connor told a female colleague in October 2024 that he “hope[d] you get raped on your way to Waterloo”, while he was off-duty in a pub. The incident was reported as part of a witness appeal and “proactive wider investigation” launched after the broadcast of the Panorama film. At the time, the Met police commissioner, Sir Mark Rowley, said the footage was “ vile to watch ” and featured “incontrovertible evidence” that would enable the fast-tracking of misconduct hearings. O’Connor’s sacking comes a few weeks after the dismissal of PC Lloyd Hunter, who was found to have made comments that trivialised the use of force and suggested that he would enjoy using force against members of the public. Hunter also said he “hated” homeless people. Commander Simon Messinger, from the Met’s professionalism department, said: “Two more officers have now been dismissed for their appalling comments and attitudes. “I hope this sends a very clear message about the standards we expect from all our officers and the Met’s determination to improve our culture across the organisation. “We continue to support the ongoing IOPC [Independent Office for Police Conduct] investigation.” The IOPC confirmed that investigations were continuing against 15 other officers or police staff and that misconduct had been identified from footage provided by the BBC which had not been included in the Panorama broadcast. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion A gross misconduct hearing is scheduled for later this month over comments made by a detention officer regarding the treatment of people being held in police custody. Amanda Rowe, the IOPC’s director of engagement, said: “This is one of our largest ever investigations in terms of the number of officers investigated, and the sheer number of fast-tracked disciplinary proceedings show how seriously the IOPC and the Met, who held the misconduct hearings, are treating this matter.” Both O’Connor and Hunter will be barred from rejoining the police force. https://www.politico.eu/article/how-maro.text: When Maroš Šefčovič set out his strategy for engaging with China to European Union ambassadors in July, he had a warning for governments urging tougher action on trade against Beijing. “Sometimes, it’s even popular to start a trade war, but it’s very difficult to finish it,” the EU trade chief recalled later in an interview with POLITICO. Three months on, Šefčovič has secured a first breakthrough, reaching a deal in Beijing last week to sharply reduce imports of Chinese hybrid cars. The symbolic win marks a small step toward stabilizing a trading relationship that Brussels believes has reached a dangerous tipping point. Advertisement The agreement, which will initially cap imports at 350,000 vehicles a year, marks a significant concession from Beijing, whose carmakers have been flooding the European market with increasingly competitive vehicles. For Šefčovič, who negotiated last year’s tariff truce with Donald Trump, the agreement suggests his strategy of engagement backed by the threat of tougher trade measures may be starting to pay off. Šefčovič agreed to launch the trade dialogue at a meeting with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao in Brussels in late June. By focusing initially on cars — an area where the EU has leverage as one of the few major markets still open to Chinese manufacturers — the Slovak commissioner hoped to secure a confidence-building win before tackling thornier questions, from critical raw materials to China’s vast industrial overcapacity. At the same time, he worked to coalesce European governments behind a parallel effort to strengthen the bloc’s trade defenses, reinforcing his negotiating position with the threat of tougher action to bring down the EU’s €1 billion-a-day trade deficit with China. The hybrid deal, however, is only the opening move in a much bigger contest. Advertisement EU leaders meet in Brussels on Thursday to take stock, weighing the benefits of continued engagement against demands for more aggressive action to protect European industry from a surge in Chinese imports. The meeting will test whether a commissioner who has made a career of finding compromises with difficult partners can maintain Europe’s support for a strategy whose success is far from assured. “You have to deal with the same partner across the table,” Šefčovič said of the risks of starting a trade war, in the interview with POLITICO in August . “So if you can avoid this, it would be much better.” Market power Šefčovič’s opening move was to focus on an area where Europe still has leverage: access to its market of 450 million people. China’s fiercely competitive manufacturers have become global powerhouses, but they are struggling with weak demand at home. A prolonged property slump has weighed on consumer spending, while cutthroat competition has triggered price wars. Domestic sales of passenger vehicles fell 28% in September from a year earlier. That makes overseas markets increasingly important. With the U.S. shutting out Chinese imports, Europe remains one of the most lucrative markets still open to Chinese manufacturers. Advertisement Šefčovič gambled that Beijing would prefer to accept limits on exports rather than risk losing access to the European market altogether. He set his sights on the automotive sector, where Chinese manufacturers have been making rapid inroads. Chinese carmakers accounted for just 2% of both the European hybrid and plug-in hybrid markets in 2024; by the first half of 2026, their respective shares had risen to 14% and 25%, industry figures show . The Commission was preparing to restrict hybrid imports even without an agreement. But a negotiated settlement also offered Šefčovič something valuable politically: evidence that engagement with Beijing could deliver tangible results. BYD electric cars in a dealership in Berlin on April 5, 2025. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images The negotiations were intense, according to a person familiar with the talks on the Chinese side. “It was very, very tough,” the person said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the closed-door negotiations. “Both sides hadn’t seen such intensity in a long time. No summer break, no holidays. They worked around the clock even one, two days prior to Šefčovič’s trip to Beijing.” While pursuing dialogue, Brussels also wanted to convince Beijing that it was prepared to take tougher action if the negotiations failed. Advertisement Šefčovič had earlier flagged plans for a new “diversification instrument” that would require businesses in critical sectors to source essential inputs from at least three suppliers — a move to reduce China’s ability to exploit Europe’s dependence on its critical raw materials. Then, just three days before Šefčovič’s trip to Beijing, France and Germany raised the stakes. President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called for a powerful new trade weapon that would allow Brussels to restrict — or even shut off — access to the European market within days for countries deemed to have severely distorted the bloc’s single market. The proposal did not explicitly name China, but Beijing was its obvious target. Keeping it together EU leaders are expected to welcome the agreement but also press the Commission to act quickly to strengthen the bloc’s trade defenses, according to several diplomats. The understanding reached in Beijing has bought time, but hasn’t settled how far Brussels should go if Chinese exports keep rising or negotiations stall. “We’re losing thousands of jobs in industry; olive oil and ice cream won’t solve the core issue,” said one EU diplomat after Šefčovič briefed ambassadors on Sunday, referring to reported deliverables from the talks. Advertisement A senior German official welcomed the Beijing deal as a first step in the right direction. “It’s a positive sign — which, of course, doesn’t fully solve the problem of the trade deficit with China,” the official said. But Berlin’s support for a tougher line might prove short-lived. Alicia García-Herrero, a senior fellow at the Bruegel think tank, argued that Beijing’s concessions had been calculated to assuage Berlin, given the importance of the automotive industry to the German economy. Production line at the Stellantis multinational car manufacturer’s plant in Poissy, France on April 15, 2026. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images “I’m just hoping Merz doesn’t turn away from the letter he sent to the Commission,” she said. With the German chancellor politically weakened at home, García-Herrero fears he may be reluctant to risk a prolonged confrontation: “I worry Merz will take this quick win and run.” That leaves Šefčovič facing a balancing act: keeping EU governments on board with continued engagement with China while maintaining a credible threat of tougher action if the talks break down. “I expect [leaders] to give the Commission a nod to move ahead with other trade defense measures. China may see this as a betrayal. If that is the case, we could return to conflict very quickly,” said Noah Barkin, a senior adviser at the Rhodium Group’s China practice. Advertisement The battle ahead For Šefčovič, the challenge now is to turn a limited breakthrough on cars into a broader rebalancing of trade with China — while buying Europe time to strengthen its defenses should the negotiations fail. “There is an argument for doing to China what China had done to Europe for years — bogging Beijing down in dialogue and process while Europe gets its tools in place. But the EU needs to make full use of the time that these talks provide,” said Rhodium’s Barkin. The trade chief is expected to hold a video call with Wang in January, before the two meet again next March. Those talks will test whether Beijing is prepared to make further concessions in sectors where European industry is increasingly on the defensive, including chemicals . Another priority is critical raw materials, where China has agreed to continue issuing export licenses for rare earths. Beijing’s grip on their supply gives it considerable leverage over European manufacturers , underscoring the limits of Šefčovič’s negotiating position. The Commission is also preparing two proposals for December: the diversification instrument, aimed at reducing dependence on Chinese supplies, and a mechanism to shield European industries and regions from retaliation. The scale of the challenge is daunting. Chinese hybrid imports were worth €6.7 billion in the first half of 2026, against an EU-China trade deficit of €360 billion last year. The agreement offers some relief to European automakers but does little to address the underlying imbalance. Advertisement Brussels hopes the hybrid safeguard can serve as a blueprint for protecting other industries facing a surge in Chinese imports. “We hear our industry. That includes the chemical industry, the wind industry, the furniture industry. We know where there’s a surge, and we know what hits the hardest in terms of our deindustrialization,” a senior Commission official said on Monday. Šefčovič acknowledged the limits of dialogue in his August interview, warning that negotiations would become harder to sustain without tangible progress. “What would be very important is to come back to say there is acknowledgment of the issue and there are already some pilot schemes which we want to test and to see if they are working,” he said. “But if simply there will be no action, then of course it will be much more difficult for us just to talk about these issues.” Jordyn Dahl in Brussels and Hans von der Burchard in Berlin contributed reporting.

Starting from its capital Budapest, you need to travel more than 500 kilometers, cross into neighboring Croatia and wind through mountains until you reach the nearest stretch of the Adriatic Sea. Yet if you step into the Hungarian Natural History Museum in Budapest, the sea is remarkably close. Beneath the soaring roof of the museum's entrance hall, even before the ticket counter, hangs the skeleton of a fin whale more than 20 meters long and weighing over 2 metric tons. The whale was caught in the Atlantic in 1896 and its skeleton, first displayed in Vienna, eventually found its way to Hungary. Over the more than 100 years that followed, it survived a fire caused by an artillery shell explosion in 1956, and was moved into the museum's present building in 2004. The architectural design had to factor in the whale, with the ceiling designed asymmetrically to make room for the giant skeleton. By placing such a legendary specimen at its entrance, the museum implies to all visitors its longing for the sea and offers clues leading to more ocean-related collections inside. Ocean discovery When you walk farther inside, another marine world appears — this time beneath your feet. A 122-square-meter glass floor covers a reconstruction of a coral reef, with fish exhibits lying about 60 centimeters below visitors. Just look down through the glass, and it feels like walking over a shallow tropical sea. The display recreates several different reef environments, from fringing and patch reefs to barrier reefs and deeper waters. Around it, aquariums built into the walls contain live fish and corals, which hold about 13,000 liters of water together, or roughly the volume of 70 bathtubs. According to information displayed at the museum, this permanent exhibition contains more than 200 coral species, around 160 fish species and over 1,000 specimens and living examples of mollusks, crustaceans, worms, sea urchins, starfish and other creatures. Above the coral exhibition is a playful gallery constructed in the shape of Noah's Ark, where a furry giraffe pokes its head through a window high above visitors. Monkeys, ostriches and tigers also appear among the animals supposedly sheltering aboard the vessel. But this Hungarian version of the ark has apparently made room for sea creatures as well: inside its cabin there are shelves displaying shells, conchs and other marine creatures. Hungarians, it seems, have a way of keeping the sea close. That fascination is also embodied in some displayed items that come from the distant past. On the other side, opposite the ark is another exhibition, "Lost Worlds — The Age of Dinosaurs in Hungary", which displays a collection of fossils discovered in the country. Among the most memorable fossils on display is that of a marine crocodile that lived about 180 million years ago. Only part of the prehistoric animal survives, principally sections of its vertebral column and ribs. But the museum has reconstructed the creature around those remains, presenting a predator roughly 5 meters long in a hunting pose. Its body immediately reveals that this was no ordinary crocodile. Its small limbs, long paddle-like tail and extremely sharp teeth all tell audiences it was an animal adapted for life in the sea. The label beside the ocean crocodile reads: Place: Hungary. Age: 180 million years. In other words, today's landlocked Hungary was once covered by the sea. To understand how a marine predator could end up fossilized in the middle of a landlocked European country, you need to board a time machine and travel back about 180 million years. The map of the world then is quite different from today's. The supercontinent, Pangaea, had begun breaking apart. Between its great northern and southern landmasses stretched an enormous body of water known as the Tethys Ocean. The region that would eventually become Hungary was a small corner of this changing tropical and subtropical world, where islands, shallow marine platforms and deeper basins existed side by side. Conifers, cycads and ferns grew on the islands. Ammonites and fish filled the surrounding waters. Marine reptiles occupied ecological niches that would one day belong to different animals, but at that time they were indisputably the rulers. The marine crocodile displayed in Budapest was among the large predators inhabiting the region's shallow waters, while the world farther offshore in the Tethys Ocean was ruled by even larger beasts. Ichthyosaurs approaching 10 meters in length occupied the upper levels of the food chain, while long-necked plesiosaurs and large marine crocodiles moved between islands, shallow seas and deeper basins. It was a world that lasted for tens of millions of years, but still lost its standing to time. As the Tethys gradually contracted, sediments on its floor were compressed, folded and lifted, leading different blocks of crust to migrate and join together. By about 85 million years ago, parts of what is now western Hungary had become relatively stable land crossed by rivers and floodplains. Dinosaur succession The marine crocodiles were gone together with the shallow marine waters, their place taken by another group of giants — Hungarosaurus tormai, the first dinosaur to be scientifically described from fossils found in present-day Hungary, a species named after the country itself. The dinosaur was discovered at a former bauxite mine in Iharkut, western Hungary. Hungarian paleontologist Attila Osi and fossil hunter Andras Torma found the site in 2000, and subsequent excavations uncovered remarkably complete remains of the armored dinosaur. Osi formally described it as a new species in 2005, naming it after the nation Hungary and the scientist Torma. About 4 meters long, Hungarosaurus tormai was hardly a giant by dinosaur standards, but plates of bone covered its body from neck to tail, giving the compact herbivore lots of protection from neighboring carnivores. Hungarosaurus lived around 84 million years ago, during the Late Cretaceous period, and is particularly significant because its remains were among the first dinosaur body fossils discovered in Hungary. The herbivore and the marine crocodile now share the same exhibition hall, less than 10 meters from each other. However, they would never have encountered each other in life, as they are separated by roughly 100 million years. In fact, the span of time between the marine crocodile and Hungarosaurus is comparable to the immense gulf separating Hungarosaurus from humans — about 80 million years, long enough for seas to become mountains, seabeds to become plains, and past rulers of the world to die out and turn into fossils. Perhaps 80 million years from now — or perhaps much sooner — we humans, too, will have vanished from this world, leaving behind only fossils to be displayed alongside crocodiles and dinosaurs for future visitors. Just imagine what kind of life would visit that museum.
